title: Samuel Alito and New Jersey’s Fallen Columbus Statue
text:

Samuel Alito and the Fallen Columbus Statue
The Chambersburg neighborhood of Trenton, N.J., was once a thriving Italian American community, a Little Italy of square brick tenements and bungalows in the shadow of the giant smoke-belching Roebling steel plant.
Today it’s still an immigrant enclave, although the recent arrivals are mostly from Central America. The plant shut down, and what remains of its 20th-century heyday is the Italian Peoples Bakery (“goes back to 1936”) and a curious stump of a platform where a statue once stood. A close inspection reveals that the stump is in the shape of a boat.
On a Sunday in October 1959, the whole neighborhood, including the future Supreme Court justice Samuel Alito and his family, stood alongside church leaders and diplomats to erect an image of their hero, Christopher Columbus, peering from the prow of a ship as he approaches the New World.
For the Alitos, this was a moment of pride. Trenton’s vibrant Italian American community was asserting its place in America. As Justice Alito would later put it in interviews, Italian immigrants who arrived in the United States in the early 20th century, including his relatives, were derided as foreigners. They embraced Columbus, who was born in Genoa and whose ships reached the New World more than a century before the Mayflower, because they were his countrymen. His story proved that they belonged.
The statue remained in Columbus Park for more than 60 years until Trenton’s mayor, Reed Gusciora, decided in 2020, after repeated acts of vandalism left the statue doused in red paint, to remove it, and the park was renamed Unity Square Park.
Most Italians had left Chambersburg by 2020. Many of the town’s residents, chiefly Black and Central American, decried Columbus as a symbol of slavery and genocide. “What we know about Columbus simply makes his image a poor fit for a city that is as diverse as Trenton,” the mayor said at the time.
